transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-02-02 10:00 PST · Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Dev Patel (Redwood SE), Sara Lim (Lead ML Eng, Rivermark), Rajiv Menon (Head of Platform, Rivermark), Tom Alvarez (SRE, Rivermark)

Auto-summary: quick review of TTFT numbers, streaming vs chunked, kernel impact on 50/95/99th percentiles, action items for perf runs and logs.

Topics: TTFT, streaming early-flush, sequence length distribution, kernel selection, KV/prefix cache behavior, dedicated vs hosted routing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, is the audio ok?
[00:08] Sara: Yeah, good here. Sorry running late by a minute.
[00:12] Maya: No worries. Today we'll focus on the TTFT runs you ran last week and the streaming experiment Dev pushed. Dev, do you want to kick off?
[00:20] Dev: Sure, thanks. So, recap — we ran three TTFT runs: baseline (non-streaming, batch size 8), streaming chunked at 256 tokens, and streaming with early-flush. Baseline median TTFT was ~220ms, streaming chunked median 190ms, and early-flush got median to ~160ms. 95th went from 420ms -> 340ms -> 290ms respectively.
[00:46] Sara: Those numbers look good, did you keep same seq len? Some of our traffic is longer, so curious about 2k/8k.
[00:54] Dev: Good call — the runs were primarily 512 token synthetic mix. We did a short 2k run but not enough samples. Early-flush helps on shorter first-token latency because we can send partial frames back as the KV cache fills.
[01:12] Rajiv: Sorry, just to clarify, early-flush means we stream first token as soon as top-k is stable, even if remaining tokens are still being computed? Isn't that risky for coherence?
[01:22] Dev: It's more like we flush partial output as it's generated, not approximate generation. It reduces TTFT by overlapping kernel execution and network transfer. For most of your agents (short instructs) it's safe. For long doc generation we can fall back to full-chunk mode.
[01:40] Tom: From SRE side I'm worried about 95/99 spikes. Any difference in tail between streaming and non-streaming?
[01:47] Dev: Yes, streaming early-flush reduced 95p significantly. But 99p can still spike if we hit a long sequence and a heavy kernel path (attention overhead). Kernel selection plays a big role there.
[02:00] Maya: Dev, can you summarize the kernel comparison you mentioned in the doc?
[02:05] Dev: Sure — we compared two kernel families: kernel-A (default fused-attn optimized for short seqs) and kernel-B (blocked-attn better for long seqs and KV cache reuse). On 512 seq kernel-A was 8-12% faster median, but on >2k sequences kernel-B pulled ahead and had better tail. We also tested quantized int8 on kernel-A which dropped median by ~15% cost but increased tail variability a bit.
[02:32] Sara: Hmm ok. Our mix is roughly 60% <512, 30% 512-2048, 10% >2048. So seems like a hybrid routing strategy might be needed. Can Redwood route by sequence length automatically?
[02:44] Dev: Yes, that's where smart routing comes in — route short requests to kernel-A optimized pods, and long ones to kernel-B. That adds some routing overhead but overall reduces 95/99. We can implement a policy in the pilot.
[02:56] Rajiv: What about dedicated vs hosted — for production we need predictable tail and isolation. Any reason to pick dedicated here?
[03:04] Maya: Dedicated helps with predictable capacity and reduces noisy neighbor risk; we can bind kernel-B nodes for long seq workloads. Cost is higher but gives SLO guarantee if you commit. Also we can enable reserved NVLink topology on dedicated machines which helps parallel KV access.
[03:20] Tom: Are the perf runs you did on dedicated infra?
[03:23] Dev: These runs were on a shared-hosted pod cluster that mirrors your target GPU family (A100 gen2). For final numbers we'll run on a dedicated set with same config. That will reduce variability.
[03:34] Sara: You mentioned KV/prefix cache behavior — what did you observe?
[03:38] Dev: With a hot prefix cache (many repeated prompts) we saw significant amortization — median token latency dropped further and effective throughput increased. But if prefix cache misses happen, tail goes up. For Rivermark's user prompts we need to analyze prompt reuse patterns; Sara will provide samples.
[03:54] Sara: I'll upload 50 representative prompts across those buckets. We'll tag which are agent dialogues vs user documents.
[04:01] Dev: Great. Also, streaming requires smaller network frames and more frequent flushes; SRE needs to monitor NIC and PCIe util. Tom, can you capture NVLink/PCIe counters for next run?
[04:10] Tom: Yes, will do. I'll also check for interrupts and context switch noise.
[04:14] Maya: Back to TTFT tests — Dev you said you saw ~160ms median with early-flush. That's close to our goal of 150ms TTFT. What tuning left?
[04:23] Dev: A few levers: 1) further kernel tweaks (fuse additional ops), 2) tiny-batching (batch size 1 optimized path), 3) quantization profile change for embedding layers, 4) smarter early-flush thresholds (adaptive based on token variance). We'll run focused tests per lever.
[04:38] Rajiv: Tiny-batching worries me — if batch size 1 reduces GPU efficiency, cost might spike. Any numbers?
[04:45] Dev: Right — there's a tradeoff. For your QPS, we simulated micro-batch strategy that keeps latency low while maintaining 70-80% GPU utilization via background packing. We'll share the simulation CSV.
[04:57] Sara: Also, do you support multiple model variants fallback? We want to use a smaller model during overload to keep latency SLOs.
[05:04] Maya: Yes we can set routing policy: preferred model for quality, fallback smaller variant when latency or capacity thresholds exceeded. That was part of the POC plan.
[05:11] Dev: One more note — sequence length estimation at request time helps routing, but it adds a few ms. We can estimate from token count header if you can send it. That avoids probing.
[05:22] Tom: We can include token_count header in the request. We'll need the SDK change — is that supported?
[05:27] Maya: SDK supports metadata headers; Dev will send snippet.
[05:30] Dev: I'll paste a sample after the call.
[05:33] Rajiv: On security/compliance, we need updated SOC2 docs and network diagrams for dedicated. Any ETA?
[05:40] Maya: I'll send the latest security pack by EOD today, including SOC2 Type II attestation and network diagrams for dedicated and VPC peering.
[05:47] Sara: Great. Also need encryption key flow — do you support customer-managed KMS for the pilot?
[05:53] Dev: For private we support BYOK via KMS/HSM; hosted can integrate KMS for workspace keys. We'll include integration notes.
[05:59] Maya: Ok, let's confirm next steps and owners — Dev you'll run the kernel A vs B with streaming early-flush on dedicated mirror and provide a CSV by Friday?
[06:08] Dev: Yes, by 2027-02-05. I'll include median/95/99, TTFT, token throughput, and NVLink counters.
[06:14] Sara: And we'll upload prompts by 2027-02-04.
[06:17] Tom: I'll capture NIC/NVLink during your test and hand logs over.
[06:21] Maya: Perfect. Any blockers?
[06:24] Rajiv: None on our side, just scheduling the follow-up bench with Tom.
[06:28] Maya: I'll schedule the bench for 2027-02-08 9am PST.
[06:32] Sara: Works for me.
[06:34] Maya: Cool. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the spreadsheet and the security pack.
[06:40] (end)

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-heard words; some technical terms abbreviated (TTFT, NVLink, KV). References to shared artifacts: kernel-selection spreadsheet (link: /shared/redwood/kernel-spreadsheet.csv), security pack (link: /shared/redwood/security-pack.zip).
